Abstract
Improving recommendation algorithms for the Web requires coor-
dinating interacting design choices and learning from experiments.
We present RecRSI, an LLM-based research framework that uses
mechanism hypotheses to organize algorithm discovery. Each hy-
pothesis links a proposed mechanism change to a reference design,
a rationale, and an expected observation. MechSpace derives imple-
mentable primitives and composition rules from the task source;
Research Line uses this space and prior evidence to develop and test
hypotheses; Mechanism Feedback carries outcomes and their design
context into subsequent research. This organization makes each ex-
periment inform which mechanisms to develop, revise, or combine
next. Across four initial recommenders and four datasets, RecRSI
yields average relative improvements of 8.48% in NDCG@5 and
6.88% in HR@5 over the initial algorithms, and 2.60% and 2.20%, re-
spectively, over the strongest competing result for each setting and
metric. Component and process studies link these gains to coordi-
nated mechanism choices and evidence-guided follow-up. Our code
is publicly available at https://github.com/DynamisG210/RecRSI.
CCS Concepts
• Information systems →Recommender systems.
Keywords
Recommender Systems, Automated Algorithm Discovery, Research
Agents, Mechanism Hypotheses
∗Both authors contributed equally to this research.
†Corresponding authors.
1
Introduction
Recommendation algorithms shape how users discover content
and products across the Web, from personalized feeds to online
marketplaces. Developing these ranking algorithms across different
interaction settings requires coordinating representations, scor-
ing functions, learning objectives, and optimization procedures,
whose effectiveness depends on the task and on one another [18].
With limited training and evaluation budgets, automated research
must identify worthwhile changes and use their outcomes to guide
further discovery.
Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate al-
gorithm design and experimentation. Program-evolution systems
search over evaluated candidates [10, 21], while research agents
develop and test hypotheses [6, 16, 31]. In recommendation, Self-
EvolveRec couples user simulation with model diagnosis, while
RecHarness combines direction routing with accumulated exper-
imental skills [9, 12]. Sustained algorithm discovery poses two
challenges for these systems.
Interdependent mechanisms obscure which changes to
test. Studies of recommendation architectures and interaction
search show that useful component choices depend on their task
and surrounding design [4, 23, 28]. A scoring change, for example,
affects both prediction and the scores consumed by the training
objective. Research must decide which mechanisms to change
together and how to implement their interaction. Distinct code
edits may revisit similar mechanisms; a promising combination
may span several components. Repeatedly reconstructing these re-
lationships during program search makes targeted experimentation
difficult within a limited budget.
Context-dependent outcomes are difficult to reuse.
Reflection-based agents reuse feedback across trials [27, 33], and

Figure 1: Research organization and algorithm discovery. (a) Candidate-level evolution organizes iteration around programs;
RecRSI uses mechanism hypotheses to connect proposed changes, their rationale, and experimental evidence for the next
design. Both workflows generate, evaluate, and refine algorithms. (b) Mean best-so-far validation NDCG@5 gain over the initial
recommender on the same eight tasks as Figure 3(a,b). Search repeats are averaged within each task, then tasks receive equal
weight.
CausalEvolve emphasizes organizing past experience to guide
further evolution [1]. In recommendation, an evaluation measures
a complete algorithm under a particular mechanism combination.
Its value for the next experiment depends on the tested hypothesis,
reference design, and unchanged components. A failed alternative
may challenge one explanation while leaving an earlier design
worth pursuing. Research must connect the observation to that
design context to decide what to refine, replace, or recombine.
A mechanism is a design with a specific computational or learn-
ing role, such as sequence aggregation, matching geometry, or a
ranking objective. A mechanism hypothesis links a proposed change
to a reference design, a rationale, and an expected observation. It
makes an experiment both a concrete algorithmic intervention and
a research question whose outcome can inform the next design.
We introduce RecRSI, a framework that uses mechanism hy-
potheses as the organizing unit of recommendation algorithm dis-
covery. MechSpace derives task-specific primitives and compo-
sition rules, making proposed interventions implementable. Re-
search Line develops and tests hypotheses through complementary
roles for composition, refinement, explanation testing, and explo-
ration. Mechanism Feedback interprets outcomes in the context
of the tested hypotheses and designs to inform the next research
decision. A new hypothesis can build on a successful earlier design
and use an unsuccessful experiment to choose its next interven-
tion. Section 3.4 demonstrates this process in a real research run.
Figure 1 links this hypothesis-centered organization to algorithm
discovery progress across eight tasks. The name reflects a recursive
self-improvement perspective [36]: evaluated recommender designs
and their evidence support successive algorithm improvements.
Experiments cover four initial recommenders and four datasets.
Across the 16 model–dataset settings, RecRSI improves NDCG@5
and HR@5 by an average of 8.48% and 6.88% over the initial algo-
rithms, and 2.60% and 2.20% over the strongest competing result
for each setting and metric. Component and process studies trace
these gains to coordinated mechanism choices, history-informed
follow-up, and discoveries beyond the initial search horizon. Our
contributions are:
• A mechanism-guided discovery framework. RecRSI
makes mechanism hypotheses the research unit connecting
algorithm design, experimentation, and follow-up.
• A method for cumulative mechanism research. Task-
derived interventions and hypothesis-linked feedback turn
earlier successes and failures into concrete follow-up experi-
ments.
• Evidence of discovery quality and research value. Eval-
uation across 16 settings establishes ranking gains; com-
ponent, history, and continuation studies connect them to
the research decisions and mechanism combinations that
produce them.


--- Page 3 ---
RecRSI: Mechanism-Guided Discovery of Recommendation Algorithms
2
Related Work
2.1
Automated Algorithm Discovery and
Program Evolution
Automatic algorithm design searches over executable computa-
tions, from AutoML-Zero’s mathematical operations to FunSearch’s
LLM-generated programs [22, 24]. Evolution of Heuristics (EoH)
co-evolves ideas and code [14]; AlphaEvolve, OpenEvolve, and
ShinkaEvolve develop populations of evaluated programs with
complementary selection and diversity mechanisms [10, 21, 26].
The Darwin Gödel Machine extends this loop to the coding agent’s
own implementation [36].
Self-Refine iterates on generated outputs, Reflexion stores verbal
feedback for subsequent trials, and ReEvo uses short- and long-
term reflections in evolution [17, 27, 33]. DeepEvolve incorporates
literature-informed hypotheses; CausalEvolve organizes outcome-
and procedure-level factors in a causal scratchpad and uses un-
expected outcomes to generate follow-up hypotheses [1, 15]. The
AI Scientist automates research from ideas through experiments
and manuscripts; its successor and AIDE organize experimentation
through tree search [6, 16, 31]. The autoresearch software provides
a compact code–train–evaluate loop with a fixed training-time bud-
get [8]. Broader reviews examine memory, skills, protocols, and
harnesses as externalized agent capabilities [38], and analyze agen-
tic data generation through accuracy, complexity, and diversity [35].
AgentNAS builds interchangeable module slots; FairNAD struc-
tures literature-derived design attributes [5, 25]. MechSpace derives
task-specific mechanism specifications and composition rules, con-
necting a proposed research question to an implementable inter-
vention.
2.2
Automated Research for Recommender
Systems
RecBole provides unified implementations and protocols [37]; sys-
tematic studies underline the importance of tuning and comparable
evaluations [2, 23]. AutoFIS selects feature interactions, and Au-
toCTR searches their architectural combinations [13, 28].
LLMs support multiple stages of recommendation, from feature
modeling and ranking to pipeline control [11]. Self-EvolveRec cou-
ples simulated-user critiques with model diagnostics [9]. RecHar-
ness combines bandit routing with accumulated Experiment Skills,
grouped trials, validation-based reward updates, and structural
jumps followed by local retuning [12]. EvoRec distills methodolo-
gies from experiment memory; AgentX-Model coordinates repro-
duction, follow-up, composition, and diagnosis [20, 32]. RecRSI
organizes recommendation research around a mechanism hypothe-
sis specifying an implementable intervention, its reference design,
a rationale, and an expected observation. This hypothesis guides
candidate construction and links the resulting evidence to the mech-
anisms changed and held fixed, informing which designs to refine
or recombine next.
3
Methodology
RecRSI carries a mechanism hypothesis through formulation, im-
plementation, evaluation, and follow-up. Together, its three stages
connect a research question to an executable intervention and turn
the outcome into evidence for the next decision (Figure 2).
3.1
Task and Mechanism Hypotheses
Given an initial recommendation algorithm 𝐴0, a task environment
T, and a budget 𝐵, RecRSI searches for an improved algorithm
implementation. Researchers supply the initial source, data splits,
editable interfaces, and a fixed training–evaluation protocol Π:
𝜃𝐴= TrainΠ(𝐴; 𝐷tr),
𝑞(𝐴) = EvalΠ(𝐴,𝜃𝐴; 𝐷val).
(1)
The inner process learns parameters; the outer process changes the
algorithm under limits on experimental opportunities and resources.
RecRSI returns the highest-scoring evaluated algorithm, including
𝐴0 among the candidates.
A composition 𝐶describes the mechanisms used together and
their relationships. A mechanism hypothesis is ℎ𝑡= (𝐶ref
𝑡,𝐶𝑡, 𝜌𝑡,
𝜖𝑡): the reference design, proposed composition, research rationale,
and expected observation. The transition from 𝐶ref
𝑡
to 𝐶𝑡specifies
which mechanisms stay unchanged and which are added, replaced,
or removed; 𝜌𝑡and 𝜖𝑡state why this intervention merits an ex-
periment and what it is expected to reveal. The hypothesis guides
implementation of candidate 𝐴𝑡; b
𝐶𝑡denotes the composition de-
scribed in the implemented candidate’s record.
The research state R𝑡= (H𝑡, U𝑡,𝐴★
𝑡) contains hypothesis–
experiment records, open questions, and the current best algorithm.
Records store both the construction references and the observations
motivating follow-up hypotheses.
3.2
MechSpace: A Design Space for Mechanism
Hypotheses
MechSpace converts the initial source and task interfaces into a
mechanism space ST = (PT, ΓT) of primitives and composition
rules. Each primitive connects a computational or learning effect to
a source location, input and output types, parameters, and imple-
mentation requirements. Its effect path specifies how the changed
computation participates in training or prediction.
Within the supplied edit scope and composition limits, an LLM
generator proposes primitives, parameter settings, source anchors,
and compatibility rules. An LLM reviewer examines coverage,
redundancy, composability, and effect paths from the supplied
source; a deterministic assembler validates schemas, mutation
targets, and composition constraints to produce the registry and
grammar. Effect-path assessment is source-based LLM review;
candidate execution is checked separately during qualification. For
example, the reviewer rejects an evaluation-only learned readout
because the training loss does not use its new parameters. The
MoRec/CDs space covers representation, scoring, objective, update,
architecture, and sampling; it is built once and reused through task
adapters.
Composing interventions. The grammar determines how primi-
tives can be combined. In the MoRec/CDs instance, SELECT chooses
one primitive, and COMPOSE combines two or three from distinct
axes, subject to mutation-target constraints. The primitive score_
cosine_temp changes Model.predict_score, shared by training
and candidate evaluation. The primitive obj_pairwise_margin

3.3
Research Line: Advancing Mechanism
Hypotheses
Four complementary roles form a hypothesis pool Q from the
mechanism space and research state (Algorithm 1). The Mechanism
Composer proposes combinations with a joint rationale; the Lineage
Refiner develops an existing direction; the Falsification Designer
formulates contrasts between explanations; and the Frontier Archi-
tect identifies underexplored directions while considering its peers’
proposals.
From a hypothesis to a complete design. Selected primitives spec-
ify the intervention; the reference candidate specifies the surround-
ing design. A scoring hypothesis, for example, also identifies the ob-
jective to use or restore when revisiting an earlier branch. The task
adapter resolves this complete composition against the mechanism
Algorithm 1 Mechanism-guided recommendation research
Require: Initial algorithm 𝐴0, task T, budget 𝐵
1: S ←MechSpace(𝐴0, T)
2: R ←Initialize(𝐴0, T)
3: while research budget remains do

5:

6:
if no eligible proposal then break
7:

𝐶,𝑧) ←ImplementAndQualify(ℎ,𝐶, T)
8:
if 𝑧= PASS then
9:
𝑜←AdmitAndEvaluateΠ(𝐴, 𝐵)
10:
else
11:
𝑜←QualificationFailure(𝑧)
⊲skip evaluation

end if

𝑒←Feedback(T,ℎ, b
𝐶,𝑜; R)

15: end while
16: return Current best algorithm in R
space and editable interfaces. Feasibility checks enforce composi-
tion rules and reference links; candidate identities support duplicate
filtering.
The roles adapt their hypotheses to the available evidence; a
fixed selector allocates experimental opportunities. Within each
opportunity block, it enforces role coverage at the opening positions
and whenever the remaining positions are needed to cover available,
unselected roles. Other choices follow a fixed role-priority order
with stable tie-breaking, reserving opportunities for complementary
research actions.

Bold/underline: best/second best. Improv.: RecRSI’s relative gain over the strongest competing system, computed before rounding.
The Implementer receives the hypothesis specification, source,
and interface requirements. Qualification checks interfaces and
execution, with bounded repair for implementation failures. Candi-
dates that pass qualification and resource admission enter training
and evaluation under Π. An unresolved qualification failure skips
evaluation and records its status, diagnostics, and cost; the incum-
bent stays unchanged and research proceeds to the next eligible
proposal under the remaining budget. These records and measured
outcomes feed Mechanism Feedback.
3.4
Mechanism Feedback and Research State
Update
Mechanism Feedback relates an outcome to the intervention and
question that produced it. Each record links the hypothesis ℎ𝑡, im-
plemented composition b
𝐶𝑡, and observation 𝑜𝑡to the reference
design, changed and unchanged mechanisms, performance differ-
ence, execution status, and cost. The original rationale, expected
observation, and suggested tests remain available alongside the
measurements.
Using evidence across experiments. The feedback record updates
the shared state:
𝑒𝑡= Feedback(T,ℎ𝑡, b
𝐶𝑡,𝑜𝑡; R𝑡),
R𝑡+1 = Update(R𝑡,𝑒𝑡).
(3)
Outcomes update the experimental history and mechanism-level
evidence; the current best changes when validation performance
improves. The construction reference determines the base design;
evidence from another experiment can motivate a new intervention.
Role-specific inputs include the incumbent, latest result, recent
mechanism comparisons, open questions, and role history, linking
working explanations to measured outcomes.


--- Page 6 ---
Gan et al.
An unsuccessful hypothesis guides the next discovery. In a
MoRec/CDs search, round 3 asks whether the pairwise objective
from round 2 helps through general emphasis on difficult examples
or specifically through positive–negative separation. It replaces
the auxiliary pairwise term with focal-weighted BCE; validation
NDCG@5 falls from 0.3705 to 0.3438. The regression becomes part
of the mechanism history, while the round 2 design remains the
incumbent. All four roles use this observation and the incumbent in
round 4. The selected Frontier Architect proposal restores round 2’s
BCE and pairwise objective and tests cosine-temperature scoring,
hypothesizing that reducing embedding-norm effects will improve
ranking. The candidate implements Eq. 2 and reaches validation
NDCG@5 of 0.4097. Round 2 supplies the construction reference;
round 3 supplies evidence for changing direction.
4
Experiments
Experimental setup. We study algorithm discovery from four ini-
tial recommenders—SASRec [7], MoRec [34], BERT4Rec [29], and
NGCF [30]—on Amazon CDs, Electronics, Office, and MovieLens-
1M [3]. All systems share the same preprocessed data, splits, and
evaluation protocol within each model–dataset setting (Appen-
dix D). We compare RecRSI with the initial algorithms and five
discovery systems: RecHarness, DeepEvolve, OpenEvolve, ShinkaE-
volve, and Self-EvolveRec [9, 10, 12, 15, 26].
We reproduce all baselines from their official open-source im-
plementations. All systems use GPT-5.6 Terra/Luna with a com-
mon ceiling of 12 genuine evaluations, each a completed training–
evaluation run, and pre-specified API-expenditure safeguards (Ap-
pendix B). Candidates are selected by development-set NDCG@5
and retrained for final test evaluation; results are averaged over
three independent searches. The ablation study uses MoRec on
all four datasets; continuation and feedback use MoRec/CDs, and
mechanism discovery uses BERT4Rec/Electronics. These analyses
use development NDCG@5. Space construction compares final test
performance on SASRec/CDs. Reference API cost measures model-
call expenditure, and GPU-hours measure search computation; both
exclude final retraining. Appendices A–D detail evaluation scope,
aggregation, ranking protocols, feedback controls, and implemen-
tation settings.
4.1
Performance Comparison
Algorithm discovery across starting models. Table 1 reports final
test performance across 16 model–dataset settings. RecRSI improves
on the initial algorithm in all 16 settings and achieves the highest
mean NDCG@5 in 11 settings and the highest mean HR@5 in
12. Averaged over all settings, the relative gains over the initial
algorithms are 8.48% in NDCG@5 and 6.88% in HR@5; gains over
the strongest competing result in each setting and metric are 2.60%
and 2.20%. The mean advantage remains positive after omitting any
starting model or dataset (Appendix A).
BERT4Rec/Electronics links these performance gains to con-
crete algorithm designs. RecRSI reaches test NDCG@5 of 0.4046,
compared with 0.3881 for the initial algorithm and 0.3959 for
the strongest competitor, RecHarness. The eight selected designs
combine changes to scoring, objectives, and representations.
Section 4.3.4 examines how these combinations arise and which
components contribute to their gains.

Discovery quality and research investment. Across the eight tasks
in Figure 3(a,b), RecRSI lies on the quality–API-cost Pareto fron-
tier and achieves the highest average test gain. Compared with
RecHarness, it spends an additional USD 2.38 per search on average
and increases the mean test NDCG@5 gain over the seed from
4.68% to 7.36%—a 57.17% larger gain. RecRSI uses additional tokens
to formulate mechanism-level hypotheses, compose interventions,
and integrate evidence. The higher discovery quality shows the
return on this research investment. RecRSI also leads at a common
budget of 3 million tokens: mean validation gain reaches 7.72%

versus 5.09% for RecHarness (panel c). It achieves the highest test
gain per GPU-hour, 1.96 percentage points.
4.2
Ablation Studies
The ablations examine how mechanism knowledge, experimental
history, and research roles support algorithm construction. Full
combines specialized roles, explicit MechSpace constraints, and
Mechanism Feedback. Prompt supplies the same mechanism knowl-
edge through natural-language guidance instead of explicit con-
straints; Unified uses four unspecialized roles. Summary replaces
mechanism history with a general-purpose experiment summary;
Prompt+Summary applies both substitutions. Each configuration
searches MoRec on CDs, Electronics, Office, and MovieLens-1M
with up to 12 evaluations. We average the relative gain of the best-
so-far development score over the initial model, weighting the four
datasets equally.

Joint value of mechanism choices and feedback. Full achieves the
highest mean frontier gain, 5.6775%, across the four datasets (Ta-
ble 2). With explicit MechSpace, Mechanism Feedback raises the
gain from 5.1927% under Summary to 5.6775%, a 9.34% increase
in discovery gain. The space–feedback interaction is positive at
0.6064 percentage points: explicit MechSpace improves the frontier
with Mechanism Feedback, whereas its advantage disappears under
a general summary. The four-way comparison links the benefit
of structured mechanism choices to how experimental experience
guides their use. MechSpace specifies implementable interventions;
hypothesis-linked feedback connects them to the design condi-
tions and outcomes of earlier tests, helping later hypotheses target
promising combinations.
4.3
Analysis of Mechanism-Guided Research
The following studies track how earlier experiments shape later
designs, from continued search to individual feedback decisions
and mechanism combinations.
4.3.1

the better result from two independent 12-evaluation searches.
Both strategies receive 24 evaluation opportunities in each of three
MoRec/CDs blocks. Table 3 reports their final quality and API ex-
penditure.

Continue achieves higher final NDCG@5 in Blocks 1 and 3 and
nearly ties the best restart in Block 2. All three continued searches
find new best candidates after evaluation 12 (Figure 4).
Block 3 shows how earlier exploration supports the later im-
provement. Its best NDCG@5 remains at 0.3801 from evaluations 2
through 12. At evaluation 13, the next hypothesis combines the
existing recent-three-item fusion and margin objective with cosine-
normalized scoring at temperature 0.2. The combination reaches


--- Page 8 ---
Gan et al.
0.4153, exceeding the best restart by 6.92%. This scoring experiment
builds on the earlier representation and objective to improve the
design beyond the short-search horizon.
To examine how accumulated experience guides the next design,
we branch from the same MoRec/CDs incumbent with its research
history available or reset. Access to history yields a better candi-
date at each of three successive steps: mean NDCG@5 is 0.3947
versus 0.3681, a difference of 0.0266 (Table 13). After a query-gate
regression, the history-informed branch keeps the scorer and tests
item-embedding gradient clipping; the reset branch switches to a
pairwise objective. Earlier evidence thus guides both the choice of
a new intervention and the design it builds on (Appendix E).
4.3.2
Feedback-Guided Research Decisions. When an experiment
underperforms, the next decision depends on which mechanisms to
preserve and which hypothesis to test. We compare Raw, Summary,
and Mechanism at frozen decision points from real MoRec/CDs
research trajectories, yielding ten next-candidate comparisons. Raw
provides the experimental records; Summary turns them into action-
able research advice; Mechanism links observations to the hypothe-
ses and mechanisms tested and proposes follow-up investigations.
Each comparison shares the research history, available actions, and
downstream implementation and evaluation process; Summary and
Mechanism also share the feedback model and output-token limit
(Appendix C). Mechanism leads to higher next-candidate NDCG@5
than Summary in seven of the ten comparisons (Table 4).

At State 6, a convolution-and-mask regression leads Mechanism
Feedback to test a prefix-mean representation with weight 0.1,
keeping the gate and BCE objective unchanged. The next candidate
reaches 0.3755, compared with 0.3729 under both Raw and Sum-

objective, reaching 0.4037 versus 0.3673 for Summary. These deci-

build on, turning the outcome of a mechanism hypothesis into the
basis for the next experiment.
4.3.3
Mechanism-Space Construction. We test whether MechSpace
can supply effective interventions for algorithm discovery by com-
paring its generated space (A) with a human-designed space (H) on
SASRec/CDs.
To construct H, the authors examine the initial SASRec imple-
mentation and established recommendation techniques, manually
specifying mechanisms, parameter domains, and composition rules.
H defines six mechanisms, including relative-position attention,
gated FFNs, and ranking objectives, with 20 single/pair structures
and 95 parameter assignments. A contains 16 fixed-parameter prim-
itives and 494 nominal single/pair/triple combinations. Mechanism
coverage, composition rules, and space size are outcomes of the con-
struction procedures; both resulting spaces are searched through
12 genuine evaluations.
Both searches use Research Line with the same SASRec initial-
ization, data, evaluator, training protocol, and LLM role-to-model
assignments. Each winner is selected by validation NDCG@5, re-
trained with three seeds, and evaluated on held-out test data.
Table 5: Final test performance of the validation-selected
candidates from the automatically generated (A) and human-
designed (H) mechanism spaces on SASRec/CDs. Results are
reported as mean ± sample standard deviation.
Space
NDCG@5
HR@5

0.4236 ± 0.0036
0.5572 ± 0.0062
H: Human-designed
0.3540 ± 0.0051
0.4660 ± 0.0053
A yields 19.65% higher test NDCG@5 and 19.57% higher HR@5
than H (Table 5). The selected algorithm from A normalizes em-
bedding directions before adding positional embeddings, an inter-
vention absent from H. The winner from H combines bounded
causal relative-position attention bias with hardness-weighted bi-
nary cross-entropy. The comparison shows how MechSpace sup-
ports discovery: it supplies a useful intervention absent from the
manual space, which Research Line turns into a higher-performing
algorithm under the same evaluation budget.
4.3.4
Discovered Mechanisms and Research Hypotheses. We an-
alyze the mechanisms discovered in the three main-comparison
searches (RO1–RO3) and five additional searches (RO4–RO8) on
BERT4Rec/Electronics (Table 6). Each improves on its initial algo-
rithm, with relative NDCG@5 gains of 0.98–8.67% and a mean of
3.87%. The selected programs combine two or three mechanism cat-
egories: scoring and objective changes each appear in seven designs,
architecture changes in five, and representation changes in one.
The frequent scoring–objective combinations connect the values
used to learn the recommender with those used to rank items, mak-
ing their compatibility a concrete question for mechanism-guided
research.
RO2 produces the largest gain, 8.67%, by combining cosine-
temperature scoring with label-smoothed training while keeping
the encoder unchanged. The shared scorer coordinates training
logits and item ranking. Component comparisons for RO1–RO3
(Appendix C.1) expose why design context matters. With bilin-
ear scoring fixed in RO1, layer aggregation changes NDCG@5 by
−0.0014 without smoothing but +0.0015 with it. This component
comparison identifies an objective-dependent design opportunity:
layer aggregation improves the design when paired with smoothing.
A hypothesis records the intervention together with its surround-
ing design so that this dependence can guide the next experiment.
In RO2, smoothing adds 0.0019 to an already effective cosine scorer.

RO3’s pre-experiment hypothesis shows how prior results shape
the next combination. It builds on label smoothing, which had im-
proved development NDCG@5 from 0.4045 to 0.4101, and uses the
regression of a residual-head alternative to motivate a new scoring
hypothesis. The improved, smoothed design becomes the refer-
ence for testing the new scorer. A bias-free query projection tests
whether learned matching geometry can complement this objec-
tive; the resulting design reaches 0.4220. The combination exceeds
both projection alone (0.4170) and smoothing alone (0.4101). The
proposal history explains why the scorer was tested; the component
comparisons show what it adds to the design.
5
Conclusion
RecRSI makes mechanism hypotheses the unit of cumulative recom-
mendation research. Its task-derived mechanism space, reference-
based candidate construction, and mechanism feedback allow re-
search to build on promising designs and learn from both successful
and unsuccessful experiments. Across 16 model–dataset settings,
RecRSI improves both ranking metrics over every initial recom-
mender and achieves positive average gains over the strongest
competing results. The process analyses show how accumulated
evidence redirects research and develops stronger mechanism com-
binations. The resulting research cycle uses each experiment to
inform the next mechanism choice.

A
Evaluation and Aggregation
Evaluation scope. Table 1 evaluates discovered algorithms in 16
settings from four recommenders and four datasets, combining
task-specific search winners and source-selected designs retrained
on target data. This assesses final quality and design reuse across
environments. The common search cohort in Appendix B examines
progress and resources; source-linked bootstrap analysis below
assesses search variability.
Final test performance and variability. For system 𝑚, evaluation
setting 𝑡, and source-search repeat 𝑟, ¯𝑞𝑚,𝑡,𝑟averages final TEST re-
training scores of the algorithm selected by development NDCG@5.
Its design stays fixed during target retraining. Tables 1 and 7 report
means and sample SDs over three searches:

B
Discovery Curves and Resource Accounting
Search progress and investment. Figures 1(b) and 3 link progress
and final quality to research expenditure using 144 trajectories: six
systems, three searches, and eight tasks (SASRec/CDs; MoRec/CDs,
Office, MovieLens-1M; BERT4Rec and NGCF each on Electronics
and MovieLens-1M). Searches are averaged within tasks, then tasks
equally. Figure 1(b) tracks best development NDCG@5, including
the initial algorithm and carrying the best forward after stopping.
Figure 3(c) plots its relative gain at cumulative input-plus-output
token ceilings through 3 million, counting setup once and reported
reasoning and cached tokens. Panels (a,b) pair final TEST gains
with search costs; GPU efficiency divides mean relative gain by
mean GPU-hours.
Budgets and stopping. The shared ceiling is 12 genuine evalua-
tions; failed implementation or qualification consumes resources
without counting as evaluation. A USD 7–8 API safeguard, fixed
before search and independent of performance, stops searches at
the cost limit using completed plus in-flight expenditure. It stopped
18 DeepEvolve or Self-EvolveRec searches (Table 10). Counts and
costs include resumed work within each search; evaluation-budget
exhaustion and execution interruptions also end searches.
Search costs. Reference API cost includes research calls, initializa-
tion, and mechanism-space construction. GPU-hours cover alloca-
tion for qualification, each search’s initial-training share, candidate
fits, and unsuccessful attempts. Final TEST retraining and transfer
evaluation are excluded from search cost.

RecRSI: Mechanism-Guided Discovery of Recommendation Algorithms
connects interventions and outcomes to follow-up hypotheses. Sum-
mary and Mechanism receive identical facts and source diagnostics
with gpt-5.6-terra, medium reasoning, and a 20,000-token out-
put limit. The ten comparisons use frozen checkpoints from real
MoRec/CDs research runs. For example, States 1–2 come from
rounds 2–3 of the Full component-study search, and State 3 from
round 18 of a continued Mechanism Feedback run.

NDCG@5 from 0.4045 to 0.4101, and responds to a residual-head
regression by testing a new matching geometry. With query q𝑗,
tied item embeddings 𝐸, and existing output bias b, its shared
training/prediction scorer is

eight combinations. These comparisons test how an intervention’s
contribution depends on accompanying mechanisms.

Component contributions. RO3’s combination reaches 0.4220,
exceeding projection alone by 0.0051 and smoothing alone by
0.0119. Its interaction, 𝑞𝑆𝑂−𝑞𝑆−𝑞𝑂+ 𝑞0 = −0.0005, is approx-
imately additive. RO1 combines two-layer averaging (A), bilin-
ear scoring (S), and smoothing (O). Its 0.4199 exceeds all seven
other configurations. With S fixed, A changes quality by −0.0014
without O but +0.0015 with O, yielding conditional interaction
𝑞𝐴𝑆𝑂−𝑞𝐴𝑆−𝑞𝑆𝑂+ 𝑞𝑆= 0.0029. RO2’s cosine scorer (temperature
0.2) reaches 0.4379; smoothing adds 0.0019, reaching 0.4398, with
interaction −0.0007. Component comparisons use fixed training
seeds 51006, 51007, and 51008 for RO1, RO2, and RO3, respectively.
D
Task and LLM Configurations
Data and training. Electronics and Office use Amazon Reviews
2014 5-core subsets [19]; Table 9 specifies splits and ranking proto-
cols. Baseline search capabilities are preserved except web access.
Within each starting-model setting, all systems share training and
checkpoint selection; outer algorithm selection uses development
NDCG@5. SASRec: embedding 50, two causal blocks/two heads,
length 200, dropout 0.2; Adam 10−3, betas (0.9, 0.98), batch 256, 300
epochs, evaluation every five epochs, patience four. One uniform
negative per positive excludes training history.
BERT4Rec: two layers/heads, hidden/feed-forward 64/256, length
50, masking/dropout 0.2, learning rate 10−3, weight decay zero,
train/evaluation batch 128/64; 100 epochs, NDCG@5 checks every
five epochs, patience four. MoRec: batch 256, hidden 50, length
200, dropout 0.2, embedding regularization 0.005; Adam 10−3, betas
(0.9, 0.98), 300 epochs. Checkpoints are selected by development
HR@5 every five epochs with patience four. NGCF: learning rate
10−3, NDCG@5 each epoch, patience 30; batch/epochs 128/300 for
CDs and Office, 1024/300 for Electronics, 1024/500 for MovieLens-
1M.
Hardware and LLMs. Training and evaluation use NVIDIA
RTX 3080 Ti GPUs. All discovery systems use GPT-5.6 Terra/Luna.
Table 12 gives the role assignments, with T for Terra and L for
Luna. Research calls use medium reasoning with temperature left
unset. Output limits follow the task and role configurations.
Table 12: Role-specific LLM assignments.
System
Request roles

E
Research History and Subsequent Candidates
With history and History reset start from the same MoRec/CDs
incumbent (NDCG@5 0.4181), with prior experiments available
or cleared. Access to research history improves candidate quality
across all three successive decisions (Table 13). At the final step, the
history branch keeps the scorer and clips item-embedding gradients
to norm 0.5; the reset branch replaces BCE with pairwise logistic
loss.
